## From first principles to writing your own tools

### PART II — Real Programming · Modules 6–8

*Reading & writing files · errors, debugging & testing · object systems (S3/S4)*

Read a section, then do the matching exercises in `PartII_exercises.R` before continuing.

## Where Part II takes you

In Part I every value was typed into your code by hand. Real bioinformatics starts when data comes from a file — a FASTA, a FASTQ run, a CSV of variants — and results go back out to a file. That is Module 6.

Then comes the difference between code that works on your laptop today and code other people can trust: it handles bad input gracefully (Module 7, errors and debugging) and proves it still works after you change it (Module 7, testing). Finally, Module 8 introduces R’s object systems — bundling data and behaviour into your own types, like a `sequence` object that knows its own GC content. This is how Bioconductor is built, and how you will structure the tool you put on GitHub in Part V.

**Time guide.** Module 6 ≈ 6h · Module 7 ≈ 6h · Module 8 ≈ 7h. Total ≈ 19 hours.

**Sample data.** This part uses the shared `data/` folder: `sample.fasta`, `sample.fastq`, `variants.csv`, `gc_report.tsv`. Keep it inside your RStudio project so the paths in the examples resolve.

## Module 6 — Reading & writing files

Estimated: 6 hours. This module connects your code to the real world. We cover file basics, then the formats you will meet constantly: FASTA, FASTQ, and CSV/TSV. We parse FASTA by hand first — not because you will do that forever (Bioconductor does it in Part IV), but because understanding the parse is what lets you debug a malformed file.

### 6.1 The simplest reads: `readLines` and `readr`

Base R reads a whole text file into a character vector, one element per line:

    lines <- readLines("data/sample.fasta")
    length(lines)   # number of lines
    lines[1]        # ">rpoB Salmonella Paratyphi B ..."

Unlike Python, there is no `open()`/`with` dance — `readLines()` opens, reads, and closes for you. For large files you can still stream a connection, but for course-sized data `readLines()` is all you need.

For **tabular** files, the tidyverse **readr** package is the modern choice — fast, and it never silently turns strings into factors:

    library(readr)
    variants <- read_csv("data/variants.csv")   # a tibble
    gc       <- read_tsv("data/gc_report.tsv")  # tab-separated

Base R’s `read.csv()` works too and needs no package, but set `stringsAsFactors = FALSE` on older R versions.

### 6.2 Writing files

    writeLines(c(">myseq", "ATGCGT"), "out.fasta")   # character vector -> lines
    write_csv(variants, "out.csv")                    # readr: a tibble -> CSV
    cat("log entry\n", file = "run.log", append = TRUE)  # append a line

`writeLines()` is the counterpart to `readLines()`; `write_csv()` to `read_csv()`.

### 6.3 Parsing FASTA by hand

A FASTA file is header lines (starting `>`) followed by sequence lines. The idiomatic R parse uses vectorised tools, not a character-by-character loop:

    parse_fasta <- function(path) {
      lines <- readLines(path)
      headers <- grep("^>", lines)             # positions of header lines
      ids <- sub("^>(\\S+).*", "\\1", lines[headers])  # first word after '>'
      # for each header, the sequence is the lines until the next header
      starts <- headers + 1
      ends   <- c(headers[-1] - 1, length(lines))
      seqs <- mapply(function(a, b) paste(lines[a:b], collapse = ""), starts, ends)
      setNames(seqs, ids)                      # named vector: id -> sequence
    }
    fa <- parse_fasta("data/sample.fasta")
    names(fa)        # "rpoB" "katG" "gyrA"
    nchar(fa["rpoB"])

Three ideas worth naming: `grep("^>", lines)` finds header *positions* with a regular expression; `sub()` with a capture group `\\1` extracts the ID; `mapply()` applies a two-argument function across paired start/end vectors (a vectorised loop). You will reuse this shape often.

### 6.4 FASTQ: four lines per read

FASTQ repeats in blocks of four: `@id`, sequence, `+`, quality. Because the structure is perfectly regular, you can index it arithmetically rather than loop:

    fq <- readLines("data/sample.fastq")
    ids   <- sub("^@", "", fq[seq(1, length(fq), by = 4)])
    seqs  <- fq[seq(2, length(fq), by = 4)]
    quals <- fq[seq(4, length(fq), by = 4)]
    data.frame(id = ids, length = nchar(seqs))

`seq(1, n, by = 4)` generates `1, 5, 9, ...` — the header positions — and so on for each line role. Turning a regular file layout into index arithmetic is a very R way to think.

### 6.5 CSV/TSV and a first look at the data

Once a table is in, inspect it before trusting it:

    variants <- read_csv("data/variants.csv")
    str(variants)          # columns and types
    head(variants)         # first rows
    summary(variants$quality)   # min / quartiles / mean / max
    nrow(variants)

That inspection habit — types, head, summary — catches the majority of data problems before they reach your analysis.

## Module 7 — Errors, debugging & testing

Estimated: 6 hours. Code that only works on perfect input is not finished. This module is about failing clearly, finding the cause fast, and proving correctness.

### 7.1 Conditions: `message`, `warning`, `stop`

R has three signalling levels:

    message("just FYI — processing ", n, " reads")  # informational (to stderr)
    warning("quality below 20 at 3 positions")       # something looks off, keep going
    stop("file not found: ", path)                    # fatal — halt here

Use `stop()` to refuse bad input loudly; use `warning()` for recoverable oddities; use `message()` for progress notes. (Never use `print()` for progress — it clutters return values and can’t be suppressed cleanly.)

### 7.2 Handling errors: `tryCatch`

To catch an error and respond instead of crashing, wrap the risky call in `tryCatch()`:

    safe_read <- function(path) {
      tryCatch(
        read_csv(path),
        error   = function(e) { message("could not read ", path, ": ", conditionMessage(e)); NULL },
        warning = function(w) { message("warning while reading: ", conditionMessage(w)); NULL }
      )
    }

The handlers receive the condition object; `conditionMessage(e)` pulls out its text. `tryCatch` is R’s `try`/`except`.

### 7.3 Validating input: `stopifnot`

Guard a function’s assumptions up front. `stopifnot()` errors unless every expression is `TRUE`:

    gc_content <- function(seq) {
      stopifnot(is.character(seq), length(seq) == 1, nchar(seq) > 0)
      b <- strsplit(toupper(seq), "")[[1]]
      if (!all(b %in% c("A","C","G","T")))
        stop("non-ACGT character in sequence")
      sum(b %in% c("G","C")) / length(b)
    }

Failing early with a clear message beats returning a wrong number silently.

### 7.4 Debugging deliberately

When something misbehaves:

-   `traceback()` — run it right after an error to see the chain of calls that led there.
-   `browser()` — drop a `browser()` line into a function; execution pauses there and you get an interactive prompt to inspect variables, step with `n`, continue with `c`.
-   `debug(f)` — enter the browser automatically every time `f` is called (`undebug(f)` to stop).
-   `print()`**/**`cat()` **tracing** — crude but effective for a quick look.

RStudio also has a visual debugger (set breakpoints in the margin), which wraps these same tools.

### 7.5 Testing: proving your code works

**The quick check —** `stopifnot` **as an inline assertion:**

    stopifnot(gc_content("GGCC") == 1)
    stopifnot(abs(gc_content("ATGC") - 0.5) < 1e-9)   # compare floats with a tolerance

**Real tests —** `testthat`**.** The standard R testing package. You write expectations; they pass silently or report failures:

    library(testthat)

    test_that("gc_content is correct", {
      expect_equal(gc_content("GGCC"), 1)
      expect_equal(gc_content("ATGC"), 0.5)
      expect_error(gc_content("ATGX"))      # non-ACGT must error
      expect_error(gc_content(""))           # empty must error
    })

`expect_equal()` compares with a sensible numeric tolerance (so you don’t fight floating point); `expect_error()` passes only if the code *does* throw. In Part V these tests live in a package’s `tests/` folder and run automatically. The discipline to adopt now: whenever you fix a bug, add a test that would have caught it.

## Module 8 — Object systems (S3 and S4)

Estimated: 7 hours. Object-oriented programming bundles data with the behaviour that belongs to it. R has several object systems; this module covers **S3** (simple, everywhere, what you will use most) and introduces **S4** (formal, used throughout Bioconductor).

### 8.1 S3: class is just an attribute

S3 is remarkably lightweight. An object becomes a given class simply by setting its `class` attribute — usually inside a **constructor** function:

    new_sequence <- function(bases, id = NA_character_) {
      bases <- toupper(bases)
      stopifnot(is.character(bases), length(bases) == 1)
      structure(
        list(bases = bases, id = id),
        class = "sequence"
      )
    }
    s <- new_sequence("ATGCGC", id = "rpoB")
    class(s)   # "sequence"

`structure(x, class = "sequence")` returns `x` with its class set. The object itself is just a list; the class label is what lets R dispatch methods to it.

### 8.2 Methods and generics

A **generic** is a function that behaves differently depending on its argument’s class. R picks the method by name: `print.sequence` is the `print` method for class `sequence`. Define a method by naming it `generic.class`:

    print.sequence <- function(x, ...) {
      cat("<sequence", if (!is.na(x$id)) x$id else "", ">\n")
      cat("  length:", nchar(x$bases), "bp\n")
      cat("  bases: ", x$bases, "\n")
      invisible(x)
    }
    s   # now prints using print.sequence automatically

You can add methods for existing generics (`print`, `summary`, `length`, `format`) or create your own generic with `UseMethod()`:

    gc <- function(x, ...) UseMethod("gc")           # declare the generic
    gc.sequence <- function(x, ...) {                 # its method for 'sequence'
      b <- strsplit(x$bases, "")[[1]]
      sum(b %in% c("G","C")) / length(b)
    }
    gc(s)   # 0.6667 — dispatched to gc.sequence

When you call `gc(s)`, R sees `s` is a `sequence` and routes to `gc.sequence`. That is the whole mechanism: name methods `generic.class`, declare generics with `UseMethod`.

### 8.3 Inheritance

An object can carry several classes, from most to least specific. Methods are searched in that order, and `NextMethod()` passes control to the parent’s method:

    new_dna <- function(bases, id = NA_character_) {
      obj <- new_sequence(bases, id)
      class(obj) <- c("dna", "sequence")   # 'dna' first, then 'sequence'
      obj
    }
    revcomp <- function(x, ...) UseMethod("revcomp")
    revcomp.dna <- function(x, ...) {
      comp <- c(A="T", T="A", G="C", C="G")[strsplit(x$bases, "")[[1]]]
      new_dna(paste(rev(comp), collapse = ""), id = x$id)
    }
    d <- new_dna("ATGC", "test")
    gc(d)        # falls back to gc.sequence (inherited)
    revcomp(d)   # uses revcomp.dna, returns a new dna object

### 8.4 A note on S4 and R6

**S4** is R’s formal object system: classes with declared slots and types, created with `setClass()`, `setGeneric()`, `setMethod()`, and accessed with `@`. It is stricter than S3 and is the backbone of **Bioconductor** — when you meet a `DNAStringSet` or `SummarizedExperiment` in Part IV, you are using S4 objects. You rarely need to *define* S4 classes as a beginner, but recognising `@slot` access and `setMethod()` will make Bioconductor code readable.

**R6** is a third system giving classic reference semantics (objects that mutate in place, like Python classes). It is common in web and simulation code, less so in core bioinformatics.

For your own tools, **S3 is the right default**: minimal ceremony, universally understood, and exactly what most CRAN packages use.

### 8.5 Where Part II leaves you

You can now read and write the file formats bioinformatics runs on, write code that validates its input and fails with clear messages, debug it deliberately, prove it with `testthat`, and bundle data and behaviour into your own S3 classes. Part III hands you the tidyverse — the high-level toolkit (dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2) that does most day-to-day data analysis — and Part IV brings in Bioconductor, built on the S4 objects you just met.
